rationale: A wins because it does the grown-up thing: it turns the same facts into four different reporting jobs and keeps the debt caveat in the room. "Peloton is generating cash again. Its debt is still the story" is the angle B should have written instead of "The company everyone wrote off just posted its first profitable quarter in three years," which smuggles in a public-consensus claim the update never gave us. B has usable raw material, but its lead contrarian frame is how founders end up pitching vibes as evidence.
gaps_in_A: "positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow for the first time in three years" slightly overstates the supplied facts; the update says first profitable quarter in three years, not explicitly first positive free-cash-flow quarter.
"The first hard evidence the cost program worked" is a fair hypothesis, but it still needs causality proof; cost cuts and adjusted profit arriving together are not proof by themselves.
"The $200 million diet" is a little too cute. The underlying CEO-turnaround angle is stronger than the headline pun.
gaps_in_B: "The company everyone wrote off" is unsupported. No coverage, analyst sentiment, stock history, or public narrative was supplied.

"The prevailing belief is that pandemic-era connected-fitness winners are in permanent decline" invents category context from thin air. The update covers Peloton, not the whole connected-fitness market.
"Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike" makes an unsupported comparison; there is no new-bike data in the update.
"after three years of losses" muddies the accounting. The update says first profitable quarter in three years, while still net unprofitable, so the profit basis has to stay exact.
